item.title: Why Are Addiction and Suicide Attempts Treated Separately?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Why Are Addiction and Suicide Attempts Treated Separately?

Personal Perspective: Almost half of SUD patients have suicidal ideation.

Posted November 26, 2026

Key points
  • Research on and treatment of addiction and suicide are usually separate.
  • Discussions about suicide are discouraged in both treatment and peer support settings.
  • Reducing stigma in healthcare systems and beyond is essential for saving more lives.

This week I have a lot to be thankful for. Three years ago, I spent Thanksgiving in an alcohol and drug treatment center, both eager to leave and afraid to be discharged the next day. I was one month clean from a devastating, years-long addiction, and I was starting from scratch after leaving my career to save a family I wasn’t sure could forgive me. The idea of suicide, though acute when I entered treatment, had receded to arm's length.

Until last week, I hadn’t reflected on this desperation for some time. Then I got a heart-wrenching call from a friend in recovery. One of the men in our peer group had taken his own life. Like me, he’d endured many relapses, but the personal consequences of his latest setback reached beyond his ability to cope.

I had three reactions—two highly subjective and one objective. As a human, I was deeply saddened. A fellow traveler, in the prime of his life, was taken from his family, unable to disclose his suicidal urges to anyone who might have helped.

At the same time, I understood. As someone who’s attempted suicide twice during relapses in years past, I’d done the same thing as our friend, but I survived. I therefore grasped, at a level not everyone can, why he couldn’t do things differently.

Finally, as a psychologist who’s treated addiction and studied substance use disorders and suicide, I was reminded of our field’s slow progress in preventing and intervening with some of humanity’s most pressing personal ailments.

The Science of Substance Use and Suicide

Twenty-five years ago, when I began teaching college courses on addiction, it was already apparent that people with alcohol and substance use disorders are at much higher risk of suicide than the general population. Studies had placed this risk at 10-fold or higher, and little has changed since. Then, like now, alcohol and drugs were implicated in nearly half of suicide deaths.

Given these statistics, it’s perplexing that research on and treatment of addiction and suicide are mostly separate in the U.S., something the Department of Health and Human Services lamented earlier this year. Journal articles on addiction usually don’t mention suicidal ideation or behavior, and journal articles on suicide seldom mention addiction. Why?

Professional training programs in addiction are highly specialized and often independent of more general training programs for mental illness. Moreover, most treatment facilities for addiction are private and operated outside the hospital-based systems of care where we treat other clinical syndromes, such as bipolar disorder, depression, and suicidality.

Stigma in the Field

I’ve worked at and been a patient in both inpatient psychiatric hospitals and treatment centers. Patients who are fighting addiction often find themselves in psychiatric wards, not treatment centers, following suicide attempts. Understandably, staff prioritize suicide risk over addiction, often unaware that the former would never have happened without the latter.

When addiction’s role in suicidal behavior is obscured, referrals to addiction treatment are unlikely. This is especially so when patients under-report their alcohol and drug use, which is common in medical settings because patients fear stigma. Ironically, stigma runs deep in medical and mental health settings, something Nora Volkow, Director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, has voiced significant concern about.

Treatment centers often show the opposite pattern as psychiatric hospitals, with stigma toward suicide suppressing its candid discussion, even though the numbers show us that 40 percent of clients have experienced suicidal thinking or attempts.

Stigma in the Unlikeliest of Places

One might expect more openness to talking about suicide in peer support groups for addiction, but local group rules, customs, and personalities often discourage such disclosures. In my experience attending thousands of peer support meetings for addiction over the years, I recall less than a handful of suicide-related disclosures.

More recently, I’ve begun attending, as an expert observer, peer support groups for self-harm, suicidal behavior, and related mental health challenges. Although it’s early, I've heard no disclosures of substance use or addiction.

In the U.S., addiction and suicide are the two most stigmatized mental health conditions. My hunch is that peer support groups carry society’s stigma. Joining a peer support group for addiction—a difficult decision for most people—grants participants “permission” to talk about a specific mental health issue, which becomes destigmatized among members. Stigma toward other mental health issues, including suicide, remains unaffected.

The friend who called me last week recruited a suicide expert to address our peer support group. I hope it makes a difference by encouraging members to self-disclose. I, along with a colleague, have also initiated a peer support program that tackles both addiction and suicidality explicitly. I’ll report back another time to let you know how that goes.

Three years removed from my own mental health crisis, I have a lot to be grateful for this Thanksgiving. I hope you do as well.

item.title: Splitting in Borderline Personality Disorder
item.description:
Personality

Splitting in Borderline Personality Disorder

How idealization and devaluation shape relationships and recovery.

Posted November 26, 2026

Key points
  • Splitting is a psychological defense often caused by childhood trauma that interrupted development.
  • A person's capacity for nuance goes offline during splitting, causing them to see you as all good or all bad.
  • Take care of yourself by maintaining your boundaries, and do not internalize extreme interpretations.
  • Support a loved one with BPD by being there for them consistently and supporting their treatment and recovery.

Have you ever met a new friend who seemed to think you were too great? You can do no wrong, you’re the first person to ever truly understand them, you’re so much better than their other friends. But then you have a disagreement or miss a birthday party, and they seem to just…turn on you? Now they feel sure that you were only ever kind to them because you wanted something; you’re just like everyone else.

What is Splitting?

Idealization and devaluation like this are two sides of the same coin—splitting, which is most associated with borderline personality disorder, or BPD. But it, or behaviors that closely resemble it, can also occur in people with narcissistic traits, depression, anxiety, autism, and other conditions. In fact, we all do it to some degree; teenagers are notorious for it. And it happens in all kinds of relationships: friendship, family, professional, marriage or partnership.

Obviously, neither extreme is a complete or fair perception of you. The truth of who you are exists somewhere between the ideal and the devalued, but that liminal space isn’t something your friend has access to right now.

And within that inability to see the space between all-good and all-bad lies the definition of splitting. In all of us, certain cognitive processes go offline when we become dysregulated or lose homeostasis: You don’t communicate well when you’re hungry, you can’t appreciate the beauty of a sunset when you’re angry, and so on. Likewise, when your friend or loved one becomes triggered and splits, their ability to see the nuance of who you are goes offline.

Why Devaluation Feels Like Betrayal

In a way, you each experience a similar betrayal. You’re late coming home from work, and by the time you arrive, your spouse’s overactive threat detection network has them convinced you’re seeing someone else. You don’t really love them. You’ll probably leave. You’re abandoning them.

Of course that’s not what you’re doing. So, you’re likewise blindsided by their response. Your spouse is fuming because you betrayed them, and they have some choice words for you. Every positive aspect of your relationship is read back to you in a negative light. It feels like they hate you.

There is no law that says you must stay in a relationship with this dynamic. However, if you’re committed to it, then equanimity is paramount. Your key to coping is not to internalize either idealization or devaluation. Even though it feels so personal, it’s not about you. It’s about their pain and fear.

Root Causes of Splitting

It may help to think of splitting as a halted developmental process. Children learn good and bad first, and then they come to understand nuance later. But that learning can be disrupted by a number of childhood experiences, including:

  • Abuse: Emotional, physical, sexual.
  • Violence or conflict in the family: living with fighting, threats, or violence between the adults around them.
  • Inconsistent caregiving: a parent who is there for them and then absent; or kind and then frightening.
  • Emotional invalidation: their feelings were dismissed, invalidated, or punished.
  • Absence of co-regulation: no one helped them learn to regulate or understand their big feelings.
  • Chronic unmet needs: specifically early needs for nurturance and safety.
  • Abandonment or neglect: caregivers were not present or available.

Triggers for Splitting

When a person’s emotional development was disrupted in this way, their brain is quick to interpret small things as threats, such as:

  • Constructive criticism --> rejection: “They’re going to fire me.”
  • Neutral expression or flat tone --> anger: “She’s mad at me.”
  • Being asked for a favor --> being used: “He only likes me for what I can do for him.”
  • A raised voice --> abuse: “They’re going to hurt me. I’m not safe.”
  • Forgetting a detail they shared --> disappointment: “You don’t care.”
  • Being interrupted --> not mattering: “I’m invisible to these people.”

It’s not willful, and that’s important for any person who loves someone with BPD to know. In most cases, people with borderline personality disorder experienced feeling chronically unsafe, uncared for, or unseen during an important developmental stage. Their brain is hyper-wired to detect this type of threat and respond defensively.

What Can You Do?

You’re under no obligation to engage in any relationship that doesn’t work for you. You decide what’s okay for you, and it’s a neutral choice. No one has to be right or wrong. And if a relationship ever involves threats or physical harm, that crosses a line no diagnosis excuses. Leave the situation and get help right away.

If you’re safe and you choose to stay involved: First, know that borderline personality disorder is highly treatable. Recovery and remission are possible and even likely with the right support. And there are a few things you can do to take care of yourself and support your loved one. For you:

  • Keep your sense of self anchored internally. Don’t accept any extreme interpretations as truth.
  • Maintain trust with yourself. Set boundaries ahead of time when you’re calm; follow through with them.
  • Pause the interaction, not the relationship. Table an escalating conversation with a reassurance that you’ll come back.
  • Have support. See your own therapist regularly; talk with friends who hold a balanced perspective of you.
  • Don’t overinterpret. Watch that you don’t also split: “They hate me. Our relationship is over.” Remember that splitting is a transient state.

And to support your loved one in feeling safe and secure so that they may recover:

  • Be steadfast. Do what you say you will do, don’t do what you said you won’t, and be there for them consistently.
  • Give context up front. “I got a flat tire. I’m fixing it now. I’ll be late, but I’ll be there!”
  • Validate the feeling. “I can see you’re really hurt that I didn’t call yesterday.”
  • But not the conclusion. If your loved one says you don’t care about them, for example, don’t litigate that.
  • Support their treatment. In whatever capacity is appropriate to your relationship with them, and with them leading.

Learned safety can rewire the fear that leads to splitting. As people with BPD build a sense of safety in treatment and in trustworthy relationships, the space between all-good and all-bad slowly and increasingly opens up to them.
